Q: Merge multiple JSON files (more than two) A:

To merge more than two JSON files, the most reliable approach is to load each file programmatically, combine the data, and then write the merged result back to a new JSON file.

Below is a simple example using Python.

Example: Merging multiple JSON files (Python)

import json

merged_data = {}

files = [
    "file1.json",
    "file2.json",
    "file3.json"
]

for file_name in files:
    with open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        data = json.load(f)
        merged_data.update(data)

with open("merged.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    json.dump(merged_data, out, indent=2)

Explanation:

  • Each JSON file is read and parsed into a Python dictionary
  • The update() method merges keys into a single object
  • If the same key appears in multiple files, the value from the later file overwrites the earlier one
  • The final merged result is written to merged.json
  • This approach works when all JSON files contain objects (not arrays)
  • If the files contain arrays, they may need to be concatenated instead
  • Deeply nested JSON may require a recursive merge

If you want to quickly merge and inspect JSON files during development, browser-based tools can be useful.

I work on Regimify, which provides a JSON merge tool here: https://regimify.com/json-tools/merge

It can help visually verify the merged output, but for production workflows, a programmatic solution like the one above is recommended.

Q: How to locate and examine stack memory in QNX OS on ARM64? A:

if I try x/1000xw 0x1a85b55000 in gdb, gdb displays hundreds of zero words

You are subtracting the guard page size from stack size. You shouldn't -- the guard page follows the stack, but isn't part of it (the picture marks both as part of "main stack", but it is misleading).

So something like x/100xw 0x1a85b16000 + 0x40000 - 400 will give you bytes at the top of the stack. Indeed we see that &test[0] == 0x1a85b556c2, which is 2366 bytes below the high end (0x1a85b56000) of the stack.

What is above test[0] on the stack?

We can't tell: often the thread library puts some kind of its own data (such as thread descriptor) there. The std::thread implementation may also put data there.

How can I correctly localize the thread's stack in the dumped memory?

The amount of data between the high end of the stack and your local variables will be constant for a given C and C++ runtime implementation, but may vary from one version of runtime to another. You can't compute it reliably.

But in your own program you can print that address and then find that address in the dump.

Q: Regex for CSV split including multiple double quotes A:

You can use the following regex:

"[^"]*(?:""[^"]*)*"

See demo

This regex will match either a non-quote, or 2 consequent double quotes inside double quotation marks.

How does it work? Let me share a graphics from debuggex.com:

With the regex, we match:

  • " - (1) - a literal quote
  • [^"]* - (2, 3) - 0 or more characters other than a quote (yes, including a newline, this is a negated character class), if there are none, then the regex searches for the final literal quote (6)
  • (?:""[^"]*)* - (4,5) - 0 or more sequences of:
    • "" - (4) - double double quotation marks
    • [^"]* - (5) - 0 or more characters other than a quote
  • " - (6) - the final literal quote.

This works faster than "(?:[^"]|"")*" (although yielding the same results), because the processing the former is linear, involving much less backtracking.

Q: How to improve `shutil.rmtree` performance on PolarDB-Filesystem over FUSE? A:

To detect at runtime whether a given path resides on a PolarDB-Filesystem mounted via FUSE, you can parse /proc/mounts and check for FUSE mount entries that match the path and have a filesystem type indicating PolarDB (e.g., fuse.pfs or similar).

Method: Parse /proc/mounts

  • Read the file /proc/mounts, which lists all active mounts.
  • For each line, extract:
    • Mount point (e.g., /mnt/pfs)
    • Filesystem type (e.g., fuse.pfs)
  • Check if the target path starts with any mount point and if the filesystem type is FUSE-based and likely PolarDB (identified by name patterns like pfs, polardb, etc.).
  • Return True if matched; otherwise, False.

Q: Highlight all values from single column A:

Plot over with the points you want to highlight calling a second geom_point():

df1 %>%
    pivot_longer(!Indiv) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = Indiv, y = value)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_point(data = df1, aes(y = gene1, col = "gene1")) +
    labs(col = "")

You can also scale up with this approach:

(dfL <- df1 %>% 
     pivot_longer(!Indiv)) %>% 
     ggplot(aes(x = Indiv, y = value)) + 
     geom_point(data = dfL[-2]) +
     geom_point(col = "red") +
     facet_grid(~name)

data from the Rui Barradas' post:

df1 <- read.table(text = "
Indiv   gene1   gene2   gene3
A   0.5     -0.4    0.02
B   1.0     0.05    -0.3
C   -0.8    0.1     0.15", header = TRUE)

Q: discord py cog on message event listner A:

commands.Cog.listener registers an extra listener via Bot.add_listener when the cog is added. It does not replace Bot.on_message like @bot.event does.

When registering a Bot or Cog listener, the Bot’s built-in on_message still runs and it will call process_commands, so you should NOT call process_commands again from a Bot or Cog listener or you’ll process commands twice.
